item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 987 as one dies in 24 hours
item.description:
One more child has died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Friday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 987.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified the latest casualty as suspected.
With the latest figure, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 888, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 99, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
The single new suspected fatality was recorded in the Khulna division and Khulna district.
A total of 1,114 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Friday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 162,262.
During the same period, 40 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 19,567.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 142,453 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 137,350 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Health minister: Measles vaccination campaign to begin nationwide
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain said a measles vaccination campaign will begin nationwide towards the end of this month.
He made the statement while speaking to reporters after inspecting Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital on Friday, where Commerce, Industry, Textiles and Jute Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir was also present.
He said adequate vaccine supplies have already been ensured under government arrangements. The first phase of measles vaccination has been completed in all districts except the hill districts of Rangamati and Bandarban.
Before speaking to reporters, the health minister held a meeting with hospital officials, senior doctors and nurses and gave directives on improving service quality and reducing patients’ difficulties.
Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain said: “Since the government took office, visible changes have taken place in the country’s health sector. Recently, I have inspected more than 25 hospitals across the country. From my experience, I can say that over the past 6 months, the quality of medical services in every hospital has improved several times compared with before, and I have found 100% attendance of doctors.”
He said: “After speaking with patients, I learned that there have been significant improvements in doctors’ behavior, service quality, food quality, bed cleanliness and the overall environment.”
Regarding the management, drainage system and cleanliness of Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital, he said: “Within the next 7 working days, timely attendance and proper duty by doctors at this hospital will be ensured. Local administration and the concerned authorities have been instructed to resolve any problems with drainage or cleanliness within 7 days.”
He also said work on other government hospitals under construction or already approved in Sylhet would be completed quickly and the facilities opened soon.
Acknowledging limitations in the health sector, the minister said: “Currently, there is only 1 doctor and 1 nurse serving every 11,000 to 12,000 people in the country. Health workers are working tirelessly day and night for this huge population. The government is committed to eliminating irregularities from the past and delivering healthcare services to the people.”
Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain said a special “mop-up” and intensified vaccination program had been launched for children who remain outside the targets of the routine immunization program.
He said many children miss vaccinations due to a lack of awareness and information.
In the previous campaign, around 24 million children were given vitamin A capsules, while a large number of children were vaccinated against measles-rubella and other diseases against a target of 18.5 million. However, some children remained unvaccinated, creating risks of measles among them.
The main campaign ended on 20 May, while the “mop-up” program for children left out began on May 12.
Thousands of additional children, particularly in Sylhet and haor and remote areas, have been brought under vaccination beyond the original target. The campaign will resume on a larger scale towards the end of this month.
The minister also warned against broker rings that mislead patients at government hospitals and take them to private clinics.
He said: “Deceiving ordinary people is a serious crime. Joint operations are being conducted in coordination with law enforcement agencies including Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), Directorate General of Forces Intelligence (DGFI) and National Security Intelligence (NSI) to eliminate this ring. Numerous brokers have already been arrested through drives at several locations including Dhaka Medical and Suhrawardy hospitals. Although it is difficult to eliminate all administrative complications and irregularities accumulated over the past 17 years overnight or within 6 months, the government is working with a ‘zero tolerance’ policy on discipline in the health sector.”
Asked about banning the sale of hydrosulfite, he said the substance is imported by the government for use in yarn factories and stopping its import would bring the country’s garment industry to a halt.
He said authorities are trying to eliminate misuse of the substance through operations.
On how consumers can become more aware, he said: “Consumers should directly ask shopkeepers whether hydrosulfite has been added to the Jilapi. If it has been added, they should avoid buying Jilapi from that shop. This is not something that can be tested immediately. The kit available to us can detect hydrosulfite only in jaggery; no kit has yet been developed to detect hydrosulfite in Jilapi.”
During the hospital inspection, Khandakar Abdul Muktadir said 3 major projects are being implemented to improve healthcare services in Sylhet.
As part of the projects, a specialized children’s hospital and the incomplete 450-bed cancer institute will soon be completed and opened. The health minister has already issued necessary instructions to complete the remaining work of the cancer institute.
The process of opening the previously announced 250-bed hospital is also continuing.
Khandakar Abdul Muktadir said: “Alongside the establishment of a medical university in Sylhet and various initiatives by Bangladesh Small and Cottage Industries Corporation (BSCIC), the launch of these health projects will bring a major and positive change to healthcare services across the region.”
Also present during the inspection were Sylhet City Corporation Administrator Abdul Qayyum Chowdhury, Sylhet Development Authority Chairman Rezaul Hasan Koyes Ludhi, Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital Director Brig Gen Dr Umar Rashed Munir and other senior local officials.

item.title: Unidentified man found dead on Dhaka Elevated Expressway
item.description:
Police recovered the body of an unidentified man with his face wrapped in scotch tape from the Dhaka Elevated Expressway in the city’s Banani area on Friday morning.
According to police, motorists noticed the body lying on the expressway and informed the police.
Later, a team from Banani Police Station went to the spot and recovered the body. Scotch tape was wrapped around the man’s face.
Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Banani Police Station Mohammad Faridul Islam said the body was sent to Dhaka Medical College Hospital for autopsy.
He said they recovered the body from the Dhaka Airport-bound lane of the expressway near the Army Stadium around 9:45am.
“We suspect that someone killed him and dumped the body on the elevated expressway,” OC said, adding that police were examining CCTV footage from the area.
He said legal proceedings were initiated to identify the deceased and arrest those responsible.

item.title: Death of house help: Three sent to jail after remand
item.description:
Three people have been sent to jail after remand in a murder case filed over the death of 15-year-old house help Mim Akter, whose body was allegedly left outside the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH).
On Thursday, Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Jewel Rana passed the order following an application by the investigation officer. Sub-Inspector (SI) Shah Alam of the prosecution department confirmed the matter on Friday.
SI Shah Alam said: “The 3 accused were produced before the court on Thursday after the remand period ended, and an application was made to keep them in jail. The court later ordered that they be sent to jail.”
He said no bail applications were filed by the accused.
The accused are Faisal Ahmed, 35, head of the household where Mim worked; his wife Rahema Khatun Reshma, 29; and his father-in-law A B M Abdur Razzak, 47.
According to the case documents, Mim had been working at Faisal’s house for about a year. Her family alleged that she had been subjected to physical and mental abuse since she started working there.
After Mim called her family and spoke in a tearful voice about the alleged abuse, her family decided to bring her home.
Police said the accused allegedly took Mim’s body to DMCH on August 12, left it outside the emergency department as an unidentified body and fled.
The following day, Faisal allegedly called Mim’s family and told them that she had stolen money and valuables from the house and fled with another boy.
On August 17, members of Mim’s family went to the accused’s house looking for her but were allegedly abused and driven away.
On August 20, after receiving information about the unidentified body, Mim’s family went to Shahbag Police Station and, with police assistance, identified it at the DMCH morgue.
Police later identified Mim by analyzing technological data and CCTV footage.
Mim was the daughter of Fazlu Mia from the Basudev Bazar area of Comilla. Her mother filed a murder case with Shahbagh Police Station on August 21.
After the incident, the accused allegedly left their longtime residence in the Siddhirganj police station area of Narayanganj and went into hiding in Demra. Police arrested all 3 from Demra’s Bamail area in a raid on the night of August 20.
The following day, the court ordered them to be sent to jail. On August 24, Shahbagh Police Station SI Mahfuza Akter, the investigation officer in the case, sought 7 days of remand for the accused.
The court scheduled the hearing for Monday in the presence of the accused and later granted 3 days of remand.
During Monday’s remand hearing, the defense and their lawyers claimed that the house help had “committed suicide”.

From a food-deficit nation after independence, Bangladesh has now become one of the world’s leading rice producers.
Yet the challenges ahead are enormous.
Climate change, shrinking cultivable land, labour shortages, rising production costs, groundwater depletion, salinity intrusion, floods, and increasing pest and disease pressure are threatening future food security. Nahid: Country is somewhat stable, but needs strong foundation
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) convener and opposition chief whip Nahid Islam has said the situation in the country remains somewhat stable, but a strong foundation must be established to ensure communal harmony, human dignity and stronger democratic institutions.
“We are still continuing that movement,” he said.
Nahid made the remarks at a press briefing after a view-exchange meeting with members of the Sanatan community at Dhakeshwari Temple in the capital on Friday, on the occasion of Janmashtami. NCP Joint Member Secretary and MP Nusrat Tabassum and other central leaders were present.
Nahid said the country had previously witnessed various forms of torture and oppression against minorities and ethnic communities, while the state or government remained silent and failed to take action.
“Sometimes, it indirectly supported them. Due to this, a culture of impunity was created,” he said.
“From that place, after the July uprising, we have repeatedly said that the judiciary must be strengthened. Communal harmony and human dignity must be ensured,” he added.
Nahid said the implementation of the July Charter and the verdict of the referendum would help establish the judiciary on a strong foundation.
“We think that if the July Charter and the referendum verdict are implemented, the country's judiciary will stand on a strong foundation. Through this, there will be a place for people of all communities in the country to get justice,” he said.
“All political forces, including the government and the opposition, must keep this in mind. The culture of impunity must be changed. Political and democratic institutions must be strengthened,” he added.
He said the country had a spiritual bond with people of all religions, including the Hindu community.
“Their festivals are thousands of years old, and the interaction of people of many cultures and religions in this delta has developed through interactive communication. Such a bond must be maintained,” Nahid said.
He called on followers of Sanatan Dharma to pray for the people of Bangladesh and the NCP.

We are killing our rivers
item.description:
The latest survey from Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA) on water pollution in Dhaka is nothing short of shocking: 424 outlets are dumping an estimated 330 tons of waste every single day into the Buriganga, Turag, Balu, and Shitalakkhya rivers around Dhaka.
To reduce this to mismanagement and oversight is no longer possible and must be called what it is -- environmental negligence on a staggering scale.
When a nation’s lifelines are treated as open sewers, the consequences are inevitable: Toxic water, collapsing ecosystems, public health crises, and a future that becomes harder to salvage with each passing year.
That out of the 424 identified discharge points, 244 are linked to privately owned factories and industrial establishments, tells us of the impunity enjoyed by industries in our country, where they have felt emboldened to continue polluting our rivers and affect millions of lives.
This feeble enforcement and non-existent accountability needs to be addressed with immediate effect.
Let it be reiterated: Dhaka’s rivers are dying because the authorities responsible for protecting them have failed to act. All the mandates, budgets, and legal powers mean nothing if there is no urgency to do what is right for the people of this country.
When 330 tons of waste enter the water system daily, “monitoring” and “future plans” are meaningless. Only decisive action matters.
The respected authorities must literally clean up their act. While the long term plan must include proper sewage treatment and enforcing effluent treatment requirements without exception, there is an immediate need to prosecute violators and ensure that sewer lines are not secretly connected to rivers.
Bangladesh cannot aspire to economic transformation while its rivers remain toxic drains. The numbers in this survey are a national embarrassment and must be treated as a call to action. The authorities must prove they are willing to act, not just talk.

item.title: If nothing changes, then nothing changes
item.description:
This past week, a city neighbourhood witnessed a violent turf war for control of the illicit drug trade. Several people sustained gunshot wounds, though, fortunately, no one was killed.
An initial probe found politically-linked drug dealers behind the violence, with the clashes apparently driven entirely by the desire to secure territory under a new political settlement.
Only a couple of weeks ago, this paper ran a report detailing how trucks carrying fruit to the city’s prime trading hub were caught in a web of extortion. Truck drivers at Dhaka’s Badamtoli riverfront wholesale fruit market face systematic extortion by an illegal syndicate that uses government-authorized parking arrangements as a front.
Operators are charged more than 20 times the official parking fee simply to access the area, with a local ruling-party leader accused of directing the unauthorized collections.
Meanwhile, Shahed Sharif, a teenager, created a website named “ghush.site” late last month to protest the constant demands for bribes he faced while trying to withdraw his late schoolteacher mother’s pension.
Numerous citizens have since shared their own grievances on the platform. Up until the afternoon of September 1, a total of 11,666 complaints had been submitted to Shahed’s bribe-tracking site, with the total amount demanded reaching more than Tk357 crore.
In addition, recent surprise visits by high-ranking government officials to hospitals and land offices have revealed the dismal state of public services, with too many staff members remaining willfully absent.
All these examples speak poorly of the state of affairs in post-Monsoon Revolution Bangladesh. Aspirations were high -- not only to get rid of an authoritarian regime but also to witness a qualitative change in the country. Yet, if nothing changes, then nothing changes.
Though currently in a very difficult position, citizens can still endure the energy crisis if they receive a credible assurance from the government that efforts are underway to provide respite from gas shortages and electricity load-shedding.
These are not systemic failures per se; they can be addressed with the right steps. But when it comes to the quality of public life, certain things matter far more.
If your neighbourhood is not yet safe for your sons and daughters to move around in, and if dens of drug dealers remain operational, what change are we talking about?
If fruit vendors charge you more for every apple you buy on the “genuine” excuse that political elements have inflated prices through illicit extortion, what change are we talking about?
If institution after institution remains infested with bribery rackets, what public services can citizens expect from a “changed Bangladesh?”
In some recent heinous crime cases, law enforcers managed to apprehend the “criminals” very promptly. But when public suspicion runs high over the authenticity of those “captures,” it speaks volumes about the growing distrust of state institutions.
This is not a sign of a healthy democracy. It is a testament to the fact that, long after the changeover, we still have not managed to rebuild institutions that have long lacked transparency and accountability.
One no longer needs Transparency International or other social barometers to publish annual corruption reports on Bangladesh; citizens are literally living through graft in their daily lives.
Shahed Sharif’s website is just one glaring example of how corruption has become all-pervasive in a society where public offices are not yet held accountable.
At the level of state governance, it is well understood that until an aggressive catalyst alters legislative, electoral, or structural inputs, systemic inertia keeps public policies, economic trajectories, and institutional cultures stagnant.
Regime change by default does not make a substantive difference unless the political leadership embodies that change.
Over the years, the political system has been structured in a way that blurs the line between the government and the ruling party.
Power elites quickly become preoccupied with appeasing a large number of beneficiaries who manage to secure positions on one party front or another.
Consequently, undue advantages in work contracts, illicit toll collections, and the drug trade become inherent to the system.
With every change of guard, one group of politicians and their sidekicks simply replaces the old beneficiaries, while ordinary people -- the main stakeholders -- are forced to take a back seat.
As a result, citizens rarely see a tangible difference in their everyday lives. They still have to navigate the open trade of illicit drugs in their neighbourhoods, unsafe roads, illegal tolls in marketplaces, and bribery for every service they are entitled to as citizens of Bangladesh.
Governments often become trapped in cycles of compounding stagnation and the status quo because their primary motivation is catering to a narrow constituency: Party leaders and cadres.
In the process, they become oblivious to the everyday challenges faced by the wider population in a democracy.
When institutions remain weak and public offices fail to provide due services, entrenched special interest groups, lobbyists, and party cadres optimize their profits from the entire state system.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Addressing safety in the country
item.description:
The growing circulation of illegal firearms across Bangladesh is becoming a threat that can no longer be treated as merely another law-and-order concern.
At a time when public confidence in safety is already under considerable pressure, the proliferation of guns and the rise in firearm-related killings make the need for effective state action greater than ever.
According to police records, at least 123 shooting incidents occurred across the country in the first seven months of this year, leaving more than 50 people dead. More alarming still, 1,311 weapons -- including rifles and submachine guns -- looted from police facilities during the August 2024 unrest and more than 257,000 rounds of ammunition also remain missing.
These figures should be a wake-up call. Illegal firearms are being used in political clashes, territorial disputes, drug-related conflicts, extortion, and criminal rivalries.
Ordinary citizens inevitably become vulnerable when such violence spills into public spaces, and people should not have to wonder whether a political confrontation, neighbourhood dispute, or criminal feud could suddenly put their lives at risk.
While the government's formation of a special unit to recover looted and illegal firearms is a welcome, albeit belated, step, it must be accompanied by sustained and measurable action.
Recovering the weapons already outside state control must be an urgent priority, while intelligence and law enforcement agencies need to identify and dismantle the networks bringing new firearms into the country.
Most importantly, enforcement cannot be selective. Political affiliation, criminal influence, or social standing must not determine who is investigated or prosecuted.
The public has a fundamental right to safety. The government must step up now -- not simply to respond to individual shootings, but to prevent the country from becoming increasingly accustomed to armed violence.

Health minister vows to make all government hospitals free of brokers
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Friday vowed to make all government hospitals in the country free of brokers.
He made the remarks while briefing journalists after inspecting Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital, the 250-bed District Hospital and Shaheed Shamsuddin Ahmad Hospital in Sylhet.
Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir was present at the briefing.
The health minister also directed the authorities concerned to resolve all drainage and cleanliness problems at hospitals in Sylhet within 7 days.
He said a syndicate lures patients to private clinics with false promises.
Sakhawat said all law enforcement agencies, including the Directorate General of Forces Intelligence (DGFI) and Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), are working together to identify and curb such broker syndicates.
“Their activities have already been reduced,” he said.
Regarding the ongoing drive against illegal clinics and fake doctors, he said mobile courts are being conducted regularly in the districts through deputy commissioners and civil surgeons, with illegal establishments being fined and sealed off.
The minister said clinics providing medical services, including surgeries, through unauthorized doctors and technicians holding fake certificates are also being sealed off.
He said he is personally collecting lists of such establishments and supervising the drives against them.
Asked about doctors’ attendance at hospitals, Sakhawat said he has visited more than 25 hospitals over the past month and found doctors fully present.
He added that patients have also reported improvements in doctors’ behavior and the quality of food served at hospitals.
On the measles outbreak, the minister said the number of unvaccinated children in the country has increased as regular measles vaccination campaigns were not held for a long time after December 2020, resulting in the spread of the disease.
He said some children who became eligible for vaccination after the campaign, as well as those who missed vaccination on time due to a lack of awareness, remained unvaccinated, allowing measles to spread among them.
Sakhawat said vaccination activities are continuing with adequate vaccines brought in with support from the World Bank and UNICEF.

item.title: Indian High Commission warns against visa touts
item.description:
The Indian High Commission in Dhaka has urged people to remain alert to unauthorized visa agents and warned against falling for false promises of guaranteed visas, fast processing and confirmed appointment slots.
In a notice, the high commission said visa touts make various false promises that could cause people to lose their money, visas and valuable time.
It advised applicants not to hand over money, documents or personal information to unauthorized agents.
The high commission particularly urged those seeking transit visas to apply directly through the official visa process.
“Stay alert. Stay safe,” it said.

item.title: Two trapped tunnel workers rescued in Nepal ‘miracle’
item.description:
Two hydropower workers were pulled alive on Friday from a tunnel buried by debris in Nepal, a rare ray of hope on the tenth day of rescue efforts after catastrophic Himalayan flooding.
Rescuers cheered as one man was pulled through a muddy opening, a video released by the energy ministry showed.
He was helped to his feet by rescuers, and later carried on the backs of the emergency workers, raising his hand as they took him towards a helicopter.
A photograph showed the second man caked in mud, his hands pressed together in prayer, as rescuers carried him on a stretcher.
“As long as there is breath, there is hope!” Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said in a statement.
“Rescue operations are continuing in all the affected tunnels. Let everyone’s efforts and prayers continue. We have not lost hope.”
Rescuers called it a “miracle” after the August 26 glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,308 people and left more than 5,600 missing.
“I am so happy, my heart is lighter,” Amir Maharjan, the brother of rescued worker Kabir Maharjan, told AFP.
The rescued men, both Nepali, were named Sanjay Sah, 30, a mechanical foreman, as well as Maharjan, 45, a mechanical supervisor, by Home Minister Sudan Gurung.
Sah, speaking on a video broadcast on Nepali media shortly after his rescue, said he had survived by chanting Hindu prayers during the days in the dark.
“What day is today? I was chanting maha mantra inside,” Sah said, adding that he believed more workers may be inside the tunnel.
“There were as many as 40 or 45 people... I told them and everyone to run out,” he said of the moment the disaster struck.
Both men were reported to be in stable condition, and were receiving treatment in a Kathmandu hospital, the energy ministry said.
Lakshmi Naini, who said Maharjan is her brother-in-law, waited outside a hospital in Kathmandu, where he was taken by helicopter.
“It’s a miracle. I am very happy,” she told AFP. “I heard he is alive through social media, and I could not believe it.”
“I have no words to express how I feel,” said another relative, Shyam Maharjan, 45.
The rescued pair were among hundreds of hydropower workers who had been missing since a wall of mud and debris swept through the region on August 26 following a vast glacial and rock collapse on a mountain on the China-Nepal border.
Searches were continuing at the Trishuli 3A tunnel where the two men were rescued, as well as multiple other sites, with at least 12 hydropower projects smashed by the floods.
Extra soldiers had been sent on Friday to boost the search operation where the men were saved.
The government had initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive inside multiple tunnels.
Nepali rescuers, aided by experts from India, China and South Korea, had repeatedly hit walls of hard-packed debris in their search for survivors.
Until Friday, none of the tunnel workers had been confirmed alive.
Australian rescue expert Arnold Dix, who has been supporting the operation remotely, told AFP that the rescue efforts were “back in miracle country” after a “week of 24/7 heartache.”
Earlier Friday, Dix said teams at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project believed they had heard a faint response from inside the tunnel.
“They believe they received a faint response from inside saying, ‘hunchha,’ yes or OK,” Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, told AFP, adding that he was en route to Nepal to join the rescue effort.
He said rescuers had called into the tunnel: “Don’t worry, we are rescuing you.”
Dix was a key adviser during the Himalayan rescue effort that successfully freed all 41 Indian workers trapped inside a collapsed under-construction road tunnel in 2023.
Dix said teams had dug through debris blocking the tunnel for 50 to 60 metres (164-197 feet) and had been hoping for a breakthrough at any moment.
Less than an hour later, rescuers pulled the two men to safety.
Some Nepali families who were searching for their missing loved ones had begun holding symbolic funerals in the last few days, in a sign of dimming hope for survivors.
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has called the gigantic wave triggered by a rock and ice avalanche a “Himalayan tsunami.”
Floods tore through mountain districts, destroying roads, bridges and multiple hydropower dams that day.
AFP reporters flying by helicopter over the valley of destruction on Thursday saw entire sections of settlements swept away, leaving the landscape resembling a puzzle with pieces missing.
Picturesque villages of green paddy fields and houses sat beside vast chunks of land washed away.
Communities near the epicentre remain cut off.
The United Nations has warned that the “magnitude of the destruction” makes delivering aid an immense challenge, with cargo drones and porters being considered to reach isolated communities.
“Access has been very, very, very difficult,” UN chief in Nepal Lila Pieters Yahia said.
Nepal’s disaster authority said the number of bodies recovered is 1,287, with 5,083 people missing.
In China, state media said 21 people had been killed and 541 were missing. That takes the overall death toll to 1,308 people, with 5,624 missing.
More than 800 foreigners from at least 34 countries are among the missing, including tourists and pilgrims, in both Nepal and Tibet in China.

item.title: Malaysia declares haze emergency in Sarawak state on Borneo
item.description:
Malaysia declared an emergency in a region of its Sarawak state on Borneo island after hazardous haze from fires in neighboring Indonesia drove air pollution to critical levels, the Prime Minister’s Office said.
The declaration covers the Serian division in Malaysian Borneo and will see 647 schools closed from Monday until at least the end of next week.
King Sultan Ibrahim “has consented to the declaration of emergency throughout Serian Division, Sarawak, following haze conditions that have reached air pollution levels hazardous to public health and safety,” Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement.
The move came after the Sarawak Disaster Management Committee formally requested the declaration when the Air Pollutant Index (API) in Serian breached the critical threshold of 500, peaking at 519 earlier on Friday.
Under Malaysian guidelines, API levels above 300 are classified as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 could trigger consideration of a local emergency.
Authorities launched a three-day cloud-seeding operation on Thursday as smoke from Indonesia’s Kalimantan region blanketed the state, driving up respiratory complaints and triggering a rush for haze-rated masks.
Emergency agencies have alerted residents and begun distributing clean drinking water to affected communities.
The government said the emergency will enable more effective mitigation measures, while cloud-seeding operations by the Royal Malaysian Air Force continued over key catchment areas to induce rain.

item.title: Trump’s White House releases deportation video games
item.description:
US President Donald Trump’s White House on Thursday unveiled a website featuring classic arcade games -- but with a “Maga” twist, in which players can deport migrants and build a border wall.
Rights groups swiftly criticized the release of the online games, which comes as the Trump administration steps up its mass arrest and deportation program for undocumented migrants.
One game called Rio Run -- an updated version of the game Snake -- features a digital version of US border czar Tom Homan chasing migrants with different skin colors next to the Rio Grande river on the Mexican border.
Another game based on the block-stacking game Tetris is called Build the Wall. “Protect the border from the coming horde,” the instructions say.
A third involves collecting nets to put in so-called “Trump accounts” -- investment accounts containing a $1,000 deposit for children born in 2025 through 2028.
The White House account on X posted a video with the “Make America Great Again” logo Maga, based on the logo of video game maker Sega.
“CAN’T STOP WINNING. Build the wall. Deport. Fill a Trump Account,” it says.
“This administration is laser focused on ways to innovate and tell the story of the President’s many accomplishments in a way that resonates with every American,” the White House said in a statement to AFP.
“This is an effort to further contrast between a culture of fun and winning and the dark socialist vision Democrats have for America.”
Rights groups criticized the White House for the gaming website.
“Makes me sick. They’ve been playing games with people’s lives for years, now they’ve made a video game of what they’re doing,” Amerika Garcia Grewal, co-director of the Frontera Federation in Eagle Pass, Texas, told AFP.
The game designers “have lost touch with what it means to be human and care for others.”
Adriana Jasso, program coordinator for Amigos San Diego Community, who works at the border, said the arcade-style games showed a fundamental “lack of seriousness” from the administration.
“The cruelty, the extremity of the administration... is no longer surprising,” she said.
The White House seems intent on dehumanizing and ridiculing migrants, even as people die in detention centers, she said.
“This presents the issue as if it were a game, when in fact it is not.”
Trump campaigned on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants and has taken several actions since returning to power aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing border crossings.
His White House meanwhile has long used social media stunts to ram home its points and troll liberal opponents, and has sparked a backlash from several artists by using their music without permission.

item.title: 81 dead as Yemen’s Houthis push towards key strait
item.description:
Clashes between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces have killed 81, military and medical sources said on Friday, as the Iran-backed rebels push towards territory bordering a chokepoint in the strategic Red Sea.
Fighting erupted on Thursday, after the Houthis launched a ground assault along with rocket and drone attacks near coastal areas, vying for control of the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait at the Red Sea’s southern entrance.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi ships in recent weeks in the Red Sea, which has emerged as an alternative route for oil exports after Iran all but halted shipments from the Gulf by blockading the Strait of Hormuz.
The rebels are now trying to cement their hold over one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes, which they have disrupted with attacks on passing vessels since the Gaza war broke out in 2023.
The Houthi offensive aims to cut off the government-held port city of Mokha, under fire for weeks, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandab, military sources told AFP.
The rebels have seized elevated sites overlooking government positions near the Red Sea, the coastal town of Khokha and Taiz city further inland, a military source and a Taiz official told AFP, requesting anonymity.
The Houthis could target ships from these elevated positions, they said.
A military official on the coast said 24 of his men had been killed, while another in the Taiz area said 15 had died there. At least 42 Houthi militants were also killed, according to medical sources in areas under their control.
The Houthis want to control the hills overlooking Bab al-Mandab and Mokha before attacking the coast, a Yemeni official in Aden, the government’s base since it was ousted from the rebel-held capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
The government has sent reinforcements to Taiz from Aden on Saudi orders, the official said.
With Iran’s closure of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandab chokepoint has gained increased importance as a transit route for oil from Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest exporter of crude.
The narrow waterway connects the Red Sea -- and, via the Suez Canal, the Mediterranean -- to the Indian Ocean.
Although the Houthis do not control areas bordering Bab al-Mandab, they hold the key port city of Hodeida north of Mokha.
In July, a fragile truce between the Houthis and the government fell apart after the rebels welcomed an Iranian plane to Sanaa, setting off a spate of attacks.
They later announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships and territory as Yemen, following more than a decade of civil conflict, became the latest country drawn into the Middle East war.

item.description:
VLSITHON 3.0, a competition for aspiring VLSI engineers, concluded on Thursday, bringing together 206 students from 106 teams representing more than 30 universities to test their VLSI skills. The University of Chattogram’s team ‘Deviation’ emerged as the champion.
‘Voltix’ from Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology became the first runner-up, while ‘Density Demons’ from Shahjalal University of Science and Technology secured the second runner-up position.
The champion team ‘Deviation’ received a prize of Tk100,000, while the first runner-up ‘Voltix’ received Tk60,000 and the second runner-up ‘Density Demons’ received Tk40,000.
The grand finale and award ceremony was held at Ulkasemi’s Dhaka Design Centre at 3:30 pm on Thursday. The event was organized by Ulkasemi, a pioneer in Bangladesh’s semiconductor industry, in collaboration with the Ulkasemi VLSI Training Institute (UVTI) and with support from American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB).
This year’s competition focused on the Place and Route (PnR) domain. Following a training phase comprising seminars and workshops, the top 10 teams were selected through theoretical examinations and assessments using Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools.
The top three teams were then selected following case-solving and presentation rounds.
AIUB Vice Chancellor Professor Saiful Islam attended the event as chief guest.
Md Nazrul Islam, secretary, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, attended as the special guest, while Mohammad Enayetur Rahman, CEO and president of Ulkasemi, was also present.
Speaking at the event, Ulkasemi CEO and president Mohammad Enayetur Rahman said: “VLSITHON is creating a bridge between academic studies and the real-world requirements of the industry.
“Many participants of VLSITHON are now successfully working at Ulkasemi and other organizations. This proves how competitions like this can help students become industry-ready.”
AIUB VC Prof Saiful Islam said: “Such initiatives involving academia and industry will encourage more students to pursue careers in the semiconductor sector in the future.”
Also present at the event were students from the top 10 teams of VLSITHON 3.0, faculty members and students from AIUB and other universities, UVTI trainers and students, and officials of Ulkasemi.

item.title: How to handle a sudden run-in with an ex
item.description:
An unplanned meeting with a former partner can stir up old emotions, but experts say composure and self-respect matter more than what is said in the moment.
Even after a relationship ends, memories of a former partner rarely fade completely. Most exes lose touch entirely, yet a chance encounter can happen anywhere — on a street corner, in a familiar café, or across a train window — bringing back a rush of mixed emotions.
Here is what to keep in mind if such a meeting occurs.
A brief smile or a polite nod is enough acknowledgment. If conversation happens, keep it short and civil. Avoid appearing angry or overly emotional.
There is no need to bring up past mistakes, hurt, or bitterness during a chance meeting. Rehashing what is already behind you serves no purpose. Seeing an ex again does not mean restarting anything — it is simply encountering a closed chapter of life. Approach it calmly.
When meeting an ex after a long time, maintaining self-respect matters most. Avoid trying to prove a point — such as boasting about how well life is going or how much a new partner cares. The goal is composure, not competition. Keep the conversation brief and natural.
Anyone in a new relationship or with a family should be mindful of that reality while speaking with an ex. Give appropriate importance to a current partner or family, without letting old ties create friction in the present relationship. Both people should prioritize their current lives.
If there is no ongoing friendship or contact has been cut off for a long time, it is best to avoid lengthy conversations during a chance meeting. Extended conversation can lead to oversharing, and situations can turn awkward. Setting boundaries is important — meeting an ex does not have to mean bitterness, nor does it mean reviving the past. Courtesy, composure and self-respect are the best response to an unexpected encounter.

item.title: Six foods that may help control weight and boost skin health
item.description:
Nutritionists have cautioned against starving or crash dieting to lose weight quickly, saying such methods can leave skin dry, dark, and dull instead of healthier.
Rather than drastically cutting food intake, nutritionists recommend adding specific nutrient-dense foods to the daily diet that help manage weight while also benefiting the skin.
A cucumber and lemon drink can be a good way to start the day. Cucumber is low in calories and high in water content, while the vitamin C in lemon supports collagen production. Together, they provide hydration and nutrients as a healthy addition to the diet.
Plain yogurt can be included at breakfast. Its probiotics benefit digestive health, and its protein can help keep the stomach full for longer, reducing the tendency to snack unnecessarily or overeat. The lactic acid in yogurt is also used in skin care.
One to two cups of green tea can be added to the daily diet. Its antioxidants support the body's metabolism and may help reduce oxidative stress.
Chia seeds and flaxseeds can help with weight control. Both contain fiber and healthy fats, and when soaked in water, they can help keep the stomach full for longer. Their omega-3 fatty acids also help retain skin moisture.
Tomatoes and carrots can be added to salads or soups as low-calorie foods. Carrots contain beta-carotene and tomatoes contain lycopene, both of which act as antioxidants and may offer the skin some protection from sun damage.
In the afternoon, a handful of almonds or walnuts can replace fried snacks. These nuts contain healthy fats, protein and micronutrients. The vitamin E in almonds and other nutrients in walnuts also benefit skin health.
Nutritionists cautioned that adding a few foods to the diet alone will not produce rapid weight loss. Total calorie intake, physical activity and sleep also play important roles in weight management. Cutting down on excess sugar, refined flour and deep-fried food is equally necessary, they said, adding that adequate water intake and regular sleep also support overall health.
Instead of starving before festivities to lose weight quickly, nutritionists recommend a moderate, nutrient-rich diet that supports both weight management and skin health.

Stateless breast
item.description:
The pain in Kulsum's lower belly was sharpening with the roll of the boat.
It had come and gone, dull and gnawing, easing for a moment only to return fiercer than before for two days now. Curled up, doubled over, she pressed her knees against her swollen stomach, trying to hold the ache in place.
Her mother-in-law, Majma Begum, rubbed at her back and her hips, though there was little strength left in her own hands. It had been so long since either of them remembered when food had last passed their lips in any real measure.
The small wooden boat had drifted on the open sea, exposed to sky and salt water alike for the last three days. Nearly fifty people — men, women, children — pressed together, lay and sat in whatever space their bodies could claim. It was winter, and even as the hours wore on, the fog over the water refused to lift.
The sun showed itself rarely, hiding for long stretches behind grey cloud.
Kulsum was folded into one corner of the crowded boat, buried beneath the weight of bodies and bundles. Whatever food anyone had carried was gone now, spent quieting crying children.
The cold bit at cracked, shivering skin until it split open. Though they floated on water, the water to drink had nearly run out; a few had only a mouthful left in the bottom of a flask, not even enough to share.
The children's eyes had long since dried of tears, but the thirst in their chests had not gone anywhere. They had left behind their homes, their land, the animals they had raised, sailing out toward an unknown destination.
For the sake of that stubborn will to survive that lives in every creature of flesh and blood, they drifted now on an endless sea. Every moment brought to them only uncertainty and nightmare.
Death might, at any instant, swoop down like an albatross and carry someone away in its claws.
Besides Kulsum, who moaned softly in her pain, lay an old man from her village — eighty-year-old Fazar Ali — gasping for breath, his lungs rattling with each cough.
A middle-aged man held him close, one hand pressed to the old man's chest, as though he could keep the man's heart and lungs from bursting out of him with the violence of his coughing.
Three days passed, and a fourth morning came. The sun still could not break through the curtain of fog. The faces of the drifting men and women had turned to plaster, staring blankly at sky and sea — two vast nothings.
Some murmured, "Allah, oh Allah," under their breath; others stared through open eyes that seemed to see nothing at all. The horrors left behind, the grief of losing everything, surfaced again and again, impossible to hold down.
There was no chance to move the great stone lodged in their chests. All they could do was try to forget, in the single effort of keeping themselves alive.
Then, suddenly, a five- or six-month-old baby began to wail in its mother's lap. Majma Begum, the mother-in-law of Kulsum, lifted her head toward the sound.
The baby's mother pressed her breast to the infant's mouth, trying to quiet him, but the crying would not stop.
Day gave way to night. In the distance, a handful of fishing boats showed their lanterns.
Their own boat carried no light at all; the moon could not reach them through the thick fog. Hunger had stolen the words from most mouths.
Silent, they blinked in the half-dark. Over the past three days, the boat had tried more than once to reach the Bangladesh border, but each time the muzzles of border guards had turned them back.
Now the engine had run dry of fuel. The boatman had let go of the helm. If they drifted into Myanmar's waters again, everyone aboard would die together.
Fear, hunger, and the tug-of-war of the will to live carried this small band of Rohingya through the trackless dark.
Suddenly, from somewhere behind, came a sharp splash. Everyone stirred — but no one could see what had happened. No one dared move from their place; if they moved, the boat would tip, and all would drown.
The sound of women wailing came from the back. Someone, surely, had fallen into the water. Word passed forward to this end of the boat — the person had been sitting near the edge, must have dozed and slipped in.
The boat was packed so tightly that there was no way to pull anyone back aboard; reaching toward one side would only tip the whole vessel over.
And besides, whoever had fallen was already far off now, carried away on the waves. The women's cries thinned into the night. The crying baby, worn out with hunger, finally fell asleep.
Night deepened further. At this end of the boat, Kulsum and Fazar Ali were both fading.
The pain in Kulsum's lower belly sharpened by the minute; it could happen at any moment now. The men nearby edged back, making room for two or three women to come close to her.
Majma Begum held her tight. The girl wept openly, thrashing against the pain. This was to be her first child. She had married barely a year ago.
Her husband, Rashid Mia, was gone now — shot dead in their own yard by Myanmar soldiers, in front of his wife and mother.
Then they had burned the house to the ground. Kulsum and Majma Begum had survived only because they were hiding in an earthen bunker beneath a tree.
Rashid had gone out looking for food, and the soldiers' guns had found him first. Later, seizing the chance, Majma Begum had brought her pregnant daughter-in-law aboard this boat.
At the other end, Fazar Ali's breathing had grown ragged, his chest rising and falling with visible effort. His forehead and the veins of his hands had swollen thick beneath the skin.
His son, Karam Ali, held his father's head in his lap, making one useless attempt after another to ease his breathing.
Kulsum's labor cries tore through the deep winter night and dissolved into the surrounding silence. The boat, riding the swell, seemed at last to be moving toward some shore — or so it seemed to Majma Begum.
The shapes of dwellings were visible now, close by. Whether it was Myanmar or Bangladesh, no one could say. They had left that question behind the day they left Myanmar's soil and set themselves adrift.
Kulsum's body convulsed with the pain, cries tearing from her throat. And at the same moment, three or four people struggled to bring some relief to Fazar Ali. Then — suddenly — a thin wail, "waa... waa" — a newborn's cry — and something like joy passed over the hollow, hungry faces around them.
These drifting people had long since lost the strength to weep. They had lost, too, the capacity for joy. But a baby boy had come into Kulsum's arms. She lay limp, spent. The newborn's cry pierced the air.
Nature is the great master; its workings are hard to fathom. As the child slipped free of Kulsum's womb into a world adrift on the sea, the pull of breath in Fazar Ali's chest was slowly loosening.
He drew his very last breath in his son Karam Ali's lap. Karam Ali held his father's still body and sat frozen, wordless, tearless, grief too large for sound. There was no strength left in his body even to cry.
Word of the birth had barely reached the length of the boat before news of Fazar Ali's death followed it. But no one had it in them to react. There was no exchange, no words.
Too much movement and the boat would tip, and everyone would share Fazar Ali's fate. And so, as though nothing at all were happening in the world — as though nothing had happened on this boat — they all sat on, bodies emptied of feeling, strangers to one another, as though they had never met, each one as if washed up from a different planet.
Looking now at his father's face, Karam Ali finally wept. Tears ran down his cheeks. Fazar Ali had once saved his son from certain death at the hands of Myanmar's soldiers.
But now the father was gone, right before his son's eyes, and there had been nothing to hold onto. With his father's body in his lap, Karam Ali drifted on beneath the open sky, on the trackless salt water — and no one on that boat knew where this drifting would finally end.
Majma Begum noticed again that the boat was drawing close to some shore. Kulsum's newborn would not stop crying. She pressed the baby's mouth to Kulsum's breast, again and again.
Nothing worked. No milk would come. At last she turned to another woman nearby — the one whose own baby had cried itself to sleep from hunger — and asked her to try nursing the child.
The woman listened. She put the infant to her breast, and the crying stopped. A small flicker of a smile crossed Majma Begum's face. But it did not last; the baby began to cry again. Majma Begum asked the woman to offer her other breast. The woman could not do as she was asked.
Tears spilled from her eyes instead. Majma Begum reached for the woman to guide the child to the other breast herself — and stopped short. The woman and Majma Begum looked at each other. No words. No sound. No language between them. But everything that needed saying passed, wordless, through their eyes.
Majma Begum asked, in their shared dialect, "What happened?"
The woman's right breast was simply gone. She pressed the child once more to her left. She gripped Majma Begum's hand tightly, and began to speak.
"My husband and I were running away together. After walking a full day, we were caught, suddenly, at dusk. They dragged my husband off. My baby — six months old — only wanted a kiss on his forehead.
"Even that much, those bastards wouldn't allow. Before they'd even gone far, I heard a gunshot."
"And then?" Majma Begum asked, with a long breath.
"They took me into a house. They put my baby down in a corner of the floor, and then they..." She broke into sobs, unable to finish.
Majma Begum tried to calm her, but the woman could barely speak through her crying. In broken words, she managed, "There were four or five of them.
"One of them, suddenly, took a knife to me..." She could not go on. Her sobbing spread through those near her. "A second one wanted to cut off the other side.
"My baby's crying — that's the only reason he didn't. They just left me there. I had no strength to walk. I tore what leaves I could find, pressed them against the wound to stop the bleeding." Her voice broke apart into weeping again.
The newborn had already fallen asleep.
Dawn was breaking. The boat had drawn right up to the shore now. Houses and people were visible here and there. Seeing the boat approach, more people began to gather.
At last the boat came to rest against the bank. A few people ran forward.
They reached out hands to help the exiles climb ashore. At first it seemed they had come to help these people save their lives.
But it soon became clear that many of them were simply seizing the chance to snatch away whatever bags and belongings they could.
Soaked in blood, Kulsum could barely manage to climb down. The newborn was held tight against Majma Begum's chest. Two other women helped Kulsum down from the boat.
The woman who had lost her breast came down too, carrying her own child. None of the Rohingya stepping onto that shore knew where they would go from here, or what they would eat.
Majma Begum and the two other women took Kulsum to a house nearby. They explained the situation — Kulsum urgently needed to be cleaned and cared for. But the man of the house refused.
Humanity, sometimes, simply stops in places. Majma Begum and her companions carried Kulsum a little further, to another house, and made the same appeal.
This time, the older woman of the house agreed — on the condition that they leave as soon as Kulsum was cleaned up. Majma Begum and the others agreed readily.
Kulsum went to change her sari at the tube-well. Watching them, something in the old woman's heart softened toward Majma Begum and her companions.
She brought out what puffed rice and flattened rice she had in the house. Majma Begum and the others were overjoyed with even this much. The woman who had lost her breast joined them too, baby in her arms. They sat together on the earthen platform outside the door, eating.
Just then, a young man from the neighborhood, Eshaq Mia, appeared in the yard.
"Have you taken in some Rohingya, Aunt?" he called out in their shared dialect. His eyes drifted toward the woman with the baby, the one who had lost her breast.
Just then the door of the tube-well room opened, and Kulsum stepped out, her wet hair loose around her shoulders.
Seeing Eshaq Mia in the yard, she stopped for a moment; the moment his eyes fell on her, something flickered across his face. Kulsum did not look up, but Majma Begum's eyes did not miss it. The other women grew uneasy too.
"Don't worry, Aunt — I'll sort them out," Eshaq Mia said to the old woman, then turned to Majma Begum and the others.
"Go on and eat. I'll arrange something and come back."
As he turned to leave, his eyes flicked toward Kulsum once more. The women with Majma Begum all understood at once exactly why Eshaq Mia was so eager to help.
Kulsum had no strength left even to stand. She wanted nothing more than a long, deep sleep. But where would she sleep? Nothing here was hers — not the sky, not the earth, not the water.
Only the shared language gave her some small comfort; at least she could speak, could try to explain what she needed.
Having returned, Eshaq Mia led Kulsum and the others to a tent — one among many, crowded with women, men, children, all huddled together with their few bundles. Even so, there was some comfort in it for those who had found shelter here: at least death did not loom over every breath. At least, even by begging, there might be a little food to eat.
Some men approached, carrying a body wrapped in white cloth. As they drew closer, Majma Begum and the others recognized Karam Ali. They understood — Fazar Ali's body had reached Bangladeshi soil after all. Without meaning to, Majma Begum murmured,
"What a fate — a whole life spent on one soil, and he found his grave on another. Only Allah understands His own design."
Days passed into months. Kulsum, with her child, slowly gathered some strength back. Majma Begum managed to bring in relief supplies, and with that, they got by.
Every few days, Eshaq Mia would come by to check on them.
But today, the proposal he brought made Kulsum's whole body tremble. By now she had heard enough that the local men would take young Rohingya women away, and days later they would return, broken. Some were taken in the evening and sent back only the next morning.
Tonight, Eshaq Mia meant to take Kulsum. He had told them to be ready. Majma Begum and Kulsum could see no way out.
After hearing his words, neither of them could swallow a bite of food. Majma Begum went from person to person in the camp, searching, but no one could offer a way forward.
In the end, Kulsum decided on her own. She would run. She would leave the tent before evening came. She told only her mother-in-law. Majma Begum grew frantic.
She had already lost her only son. Now she could not bear to lose her son's wife and grandson too. She did not know what to do.
Then, closing her eyes, Majma Begum told Kulsum her decision. She would go with her. Whatever was to happen would happen. They had already left their own homeland behind for the sake of staying alive — there was no turning back now.
Before evening fell, without a word to anyone in the camp, Kulsum took her month-old baby and her mother-in-law and boarded a bus from Teknaf bound for Chattogram.
By then they had heard that many others were already scattering in different directions, searching for work.
The bus rolled on. Majma Begum drifted into an uneasy doze, her head nodding forward each time the bus braked. Riding on toward no fixed destination, she thought they had left their country to save their lives.
Now, where would they go to save what dignity remained? Where, in all that was left of this life, would they finally find a resting place? Would her own grave, too, lie far from her homeland's soil, just as Fazar Ali's had?
Human beings, she thought, are each other's worst enemies. People harm other people for their own gain. Those who had driven them from Myanmar were human.
And those here who wished to take what little dignity they had left — they were human too. A thousand such thoughts moved through Majma Begum's mind, drifting out through the bus window and dissolving into the passing wind.
Muhammad Moheuddin is a Bangladeshi fiction writer and editor of GOLPOKAR.

item.title: Mandhana smashes multiple records with spectacular ton
item.description:
Smriti Mandhana broke multiple major records as she compiled her second T20I ton in India’s win against Hong Kong, China, at the ongoing Women's Asia Cup.
Mandhana scored a superb 124 runs off 64 deliveries, a knock that included 14 fours and seven maximums, as she overtook Mithali Raj to become the all-time leading run-scorer in women’s international cricket.
The left-handed batter now has 10,880 runs across all formats. She went past the former India captain, who has 10,868 runs across formats.
Meanwhile, Mandhana’s century was her 18th across formats, which also saw her move past former Australia captain Meg Lanning for most centuries in women’s international cricket.
Having made her India debut back in 2013, Mandhana has etched her place in cricketing history as one of India’s finest batters. Having scored her maiden T20I century last year, Mandhana had become the first Indian batter to score a ton across all formats in women’s cricket.
"I didn't know all of this happened. It's hard for my batting, to play the slower bowlers," Mandhana said afterwards.
"They (Hong Kong, China bowlers) were disciplined in the powerplay, bowled really well, and the energy they showed was something we'll learn from.
"But I love batting and am happy to contribute. There are days when you hit balls from the stumps. There are days when you edge one. It's extremely unpredictable."
When asked about her record-breaking exploits, Mandhana paid tribute to her family.
"It's been a lot of things; I would like to dedicate this to my family," she said.
"We are not really aware of them (Hong Kong, China) because we have only seen a few videos, just more about adjusting to the pace."
Having been put in to bat first, the Indian openers added 74 runs for the opening stand off 47 balls before Ruchitha Venkatesh removed Shafali Verma.
While no other Indian batter was able to score past the 11-run mark, Mandhana took the initiative to keep the flow of runs going from one end. Her knock guided India to 193/5 in their quota of 20 overs.
Chasing 194, the Hong Kong, China batters never got going, with the Indian bowlers putting on a convincing display.
Deepti Sharma led the charge with the ball, nabbing three wickets for only nine runs. Meanwhile, Nandani Sharma, Prema Rawat and Shree Charani picked up a brace each.
The win is India's second in a row and puts them atop Group A in Asia Cup 2026.

item.title: Night-owl Zverev goes distance to advance as upsets rock US Open
item.description:
Top-seeded Alexander Zverev kept his bid for a first US Open title on track with a gritty five-set victory over Quentin Halys, staying the course as a spate of upsets rocked the men's draw on Thursday.
A trio of former women's champions -- Coco Gauff, Iga Swiatek and Naomi Osaka -- booked third-round berths, along with reigning Grand Slam champions Elena Rybakina and Mirra Andreeva.
But men's third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime tumbled out, along with sixth-seeded Alex de Minaur and 13th-seeded Lorenzo Musetti.
Zverev labored util 2:15 am Friday on Arthur Ashe Stadium to shake off 52nd-ranked Frenchman Halys 6-4, 4-6, 7-6 (7/3), 6-7 (3/7), 6-3.
The four-hour 33-minute marathon followed his wild first-round five-setter against 89th-ranked Lorenzo Sonego that kept Zverev at it until shortly before 2 am on Wednesday.
"The performance was quite shit to be honest, but I won, that's the most important thing," Zverev said afterwards.
"Physically, I feel fine. I am proud, I think, to be physically quite strong. I just hope at some point I'll start playing better tennis.
"I'm winning ugly right now. It's also a skill to win ugly and when you're not playing great tennis. I think I've mastered that right now."
While Zverev survived, Auger-Aliassime fell 6-7 (5/7), 6-3, 6-2, 6-2, to 50th-ranked Russian Karen Khachanov, pulled away relentlessly from the physically ailing Canadian, who said he was "dizzy and seeing spots.
"I thought maybe it would pass, but it didn't," a dejected Auger-Aliassime said.
Khachanov took full advantage of 47 unforced errors, with eight double faults, from Auger-Aliassime, who struggled particularly on serve.
"I thought maybe he had some physical issues, it's part of our sport," Khachanov said. "From my side I tried to give my best performance, fighting, fighting."
De Minaur fell to Botic van de Zandschulp 6-4, 7-5, 6-2 while 123rd-ranked Australian Dane Sweeny shocked 13th seed Musetti 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 to reach the third round of a major for the first time.
It's not the first time Van de Zandschulp has sprung an upset at Flushing Meadows, where he shocked Carlos Alcaraz in the second round in 2024.
Meanwhile top women contenders marched on.
Fourth-seeded Gauff, the 2023 champion, thrilled the Ashe night crowd with a 6-4, 7-6 (7/5) victory over former world number two Paula Badosa of Spain.
Swiatek sailed through with a 6-3, 6-2 victory over Nadia Podoroska while Osaka survived a second-set swoon to beat Katerina Siniakova 6-2, 5-7, 6-1.
Australian Open winner Rybakina, the world number two who is closing in on Aryna Sabalenka's number one ranking, saw off Spain's Jessica Bouzas Maneiro 6-2, 6-4, and Andreeva rolled over Germany's Eva Lys 6-0, 6-2.
Gauff, 22, had lost five of her eight prior meetings with Badosa, so she was ready when the Spaniard piled on the pressure in the second set, regaining a break to force the tiebreaker.
"I knew she would raise her level. She's capable of blasting winners and blasting return winners," said Gauff, who was pleased she kept her composure.
"I think I need matches like this to build my confidence," the 2023 US Open winner said.
Swiatek, whose six Grand Slam titles include the 2022 US Open, had things mostly her own way against Podroska, a former top-40 player now 449th in the world.
She fought off four break points at 5-3 in the first set then pulled away to polish off the win in little more than an hour.
Japan's Osaka, who counts two US Open titles among her four majors, looked in total control against Siniakova as she raced through the first set and to a 4-2 lead in the second without facing a break point.
But the Japanese star's unforced errors began to pile up and doubles world number one Siniakova pounced to climb from 5-3 down and take the set.
Osaka regrouped in the decider, riding a quick break to a 3-0 lead and fending off a pair of break points on the way to victory.
"I just felt like I had to fight," she said.
So did former Australian Open champion Madison Keys, who saved five match points to beat Anna Bondar 4-7, 6-4, 7-6 (10/5).
There was a bittersweet goodbye on Louis Armstrong Stadium, where 20-year-old American Learner Tien ended 40-year-old Gael Monfils's Grand Slam career with a 6-3, 6-4, 6-3 victory.
"It's been a long ride," Monfils told an adoring New York crowd. "You are my second best crowd. Of course, it can't top Paris, but you are up there!"

item.title: Arsenal chief executive reveals 'dynasty' ambition
item.description:
Arsenal are aiming to create a "dynasty" that will see them dominate European football, according to chief executive Richard Garlick.
The Gunners won their first Premier League title in 22 years last season before suffering an agonising penalty shoot-out loss to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.
Garlick, however, told the Men In Blazers Media Network that being crowned champions of England was only the beginning for the north London club.
"There was a moment where we enjoyed it, and you saw that enjoyment," he said.
"We are absolutely saying we're not done here. This is the start and not the end. We're at the start of something big. We want to push on and win more and more. It is absolutely trophies plural."
Arsenal have never won the Champions League or its predecessor, the European Cup.
They have, though, won their opening two games of the new Premier League campaign as they bid for the club's first back-to-back English top-tier titles since the 1930s.
"I dream of us being serial champions, of us repeating what we did last year and going one better maybe in the Champions League and winning major trophies," explained Garlick.
"This is a period of dominance, you could call it the start of a dynasty, this is what we're aiming to do.
"We’re aiming to dominate football for the next few years on every front."
Arsenal face London rivals Chelsea, who've also won both their opening two Premier League games, at the Emirates on Sunday.

item.title: FIFA blasts UEFA 'smear campaign,' fights World Cup plan disclosures
item.description:
FIFA has accused UEFA of a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition" after European football's governing body asked US judges to force it to hand over documents related to its failed World Cup investor plan.
Global soccer body FIFA's divisive plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to investors, unveiled in July, triggered a huge backlash across the sport, with UEFA threatening to boycott the World Cup unless the plan was scrapped.
While FIFA quickly aborted the plans in response to the backlash, UEFA is now preparing possible legal action against FIFA president Gianni Infantino for alleged "criminal mismanagement."
Last week, it filed requests in three US states requesting the disclosure of documents related to the plan from FIFA and partners, including prospective lead investor Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital firm.
If successful in gaining access to the documents, UEFA had said it intends to lodge a legal complaint in Switzerland, saying it has been assured the case would meet the requirements to be heard in a Swiss court.
But FIFA has hit back, asking US judges for permission to contest the UEFA requests.
"While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of UEFA's smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership," say the FIFA filings.
The filings, reviewed by AFP, say UEFA does not have the right to demand FIFA internal documents because no criminal proceedings yet exist in Switzerland or elsewhere.
Even if such proceedings did exist, the filings say, UEFA would not have legal standing because it has suffered no financial loss.
The FIFA filings also accuse UEFA of illegally bypassing Swiss courts but applying directly to US courts.
Disclosure of the documents, including correspondence involving Infantino and other named FIFA personnel and advisors, "would directly threaten FIFA's interests and reveal sensitive and proprietary information," say the filings.
UEFA has made no secret of its desire to remove Infantino, who had hoped to be re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term next March after a highly successful World Cup.
UEFA may have been the harshest critic -- it described his proposal as a "shady, opaque backroom deal" -- but it has found solid support from North and Central America's CONCACAF, and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).
CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani is widely seen as the likeliest challenger to Infantino -- UEFA's Aleksander Ceferin has ruled himself out.
The three confederations have kept up the pressure and collaborated on a no-holds-barred joint letter issued earlier last month.
"Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding -- or demanding -- power to be held," they wrote.
UEFA added: "FIFA must once again be governed as an institution serving football –- not operate as an instrument of individual power."
FIFA has repeatedly disputed those claims.
"This application is yet another step in UEFA's smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership," summarizes one of the FIFA filings.

item.title: Martinelli joins Al-Hilal from Arsenal for reported £60 million
item.description:
Arsenal forward Gabriel Martinelli has joined Saudi side Al-Hilal, the Premier League champions announced Thursday.
No fee was disclosed but British media reports said the deal was worth a guaranteed £60 million ($81 million).
That would make 25-year-old Brazil international Martinelli the most expensive player to leave the London club, following Alex Oxlade Chamberlain's £35 million exit to Liverpool in 2017.
Martinelli has signed a four-year deal with Al-Hilal, who are currently joint-top of the Saudi Pro League with Cristiano Ronaldo's Al-Nassr.
"Gabriel Martinelli has joined Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal on a permanent transfer," said a statement on Arsenal's website.
"Proud to be blue, proud to be Al-Hilal," said Martinelli during an unveiling video on his new club's social media channels.
He will join Ollie Watkins at Al-Hilal after the England striker left Aston Villa in a deal worth an estimated £51 million.
Martinelli's departure comes after Arsenal sold fellow left-sided forward Leandro Trossard to Besiktas.
Christos Tzolis has joined from Club Brugge but there are concerns the exits of Martinelli and Trossard could leave Arsenal short of personnel in that part of the pitch.
Martinelli made 53 appearances in all competitions last season, scoring 11 goals, as the Gunners won the top-flight title for the first time since 2004.
His nearly 300 games for Arsenal, including 62 goals, also saw him involved in their 2020 FA Cup and 2023 Community Shield successes.
But he was left out of Arsenal's first two matchday squads of the season, with manager Mikel Arteta making it clear Martinelli would struggle for game time were he to remain at the Emirates Stadium.
Former Arsenal striker Ian Wright criticised the club's decision to omit Martinelli from the squad for the opening game against Coventry.
"The way Martinelli is being treated at the moment, it really makes me feel uncomfortable," Wright told Sky Sports.
"I know they might want him out, and a lot of people might say, 'yeah, it's time for him to move him on'. But there's ways of doing that and it should suit him as well, how he wants to leave."

item.title: Hotel Sarina Dhaka appoints Patrick Beck as general manager
item.description:
Hotel Sarina Dhaka announced the appointment of Patrick Beck as its new general manager, bringing more than three decades of international hospitality leadership to one of Bangladesh's premier hospitality addresses.
A French hospitality veteran, Beck began his career as hotel manager at the Four Seasons Hotel in San Francisco before going on to lead luxury hotels and resorts across North America, Europe, Africa, Asia and the Caribbean.
Over the past 18 years, he has held GM positions at nine international properties, including TUI BLUE Beach Resort & Spa in Curaçao, Sea Cliff Resort & Spa in Zanzibar, Hotel Ciputra World Surabaya, Discovery Kartika Plaza Hotel in Bali, and Hotel Borobudur Jakarta a 695-room flagship property frequently entrusted with hosting Indonesia's Presidency and visiting international delegations.
Most recently, he led the pre-opening of TUI BLUE's 400-room beachfront resort in Curaçao, adding large-scale project and launch experience to an already wide-ranging portfolio.
What sets Beck apart is a career that began in the kitchen rather than the front office.
A certified executive chef trained with the American Culinary Federation, he went on to direct food production and operations for Lenôtre (Accor Group) in France, overseeing more than 6,000 meals a day across restaurants, banquets and international events while leading a team of 485 chefs, including eleven Meilleur Ouvrier de France titleholders, France's highest culinary distinction before taking on the managing directorship of Lenôtre's Egypt franchise.
Backed by ISO-9001 and HACCP food-safety certifications and a proven record building wedding and banquet business at resorts in Zanzibar and Bali, this rare, hands-on command of food and beverage operations speaks directly to Hotel Sarina Dhaka's five F&B outlets: Summerfields, Amrit, Risotto, Street 17 Café and Elite Club.
That expertise arrives at a timely moment for Bangladesh's hospitality industry. Dhaka's hotel landscape has grown steadily more competitive as major international brands expand their footprint, corporate and diplomatic travel rises, and the city's MICE segment continues to gather pace.
Dining and banquet business, in particular, has become one of the most significant revenue drivers for Dhaka's hotels, with weddings, festive buffets and corporate events increasingly won on the strength of culinary quality and guest experience.
It is exactly this combination international operational discipline paired with genuine F&B and banquet expertise that positions Beck to sharpen Hotel Sarina Dhaka's competitive edge and grow revenue across its dining outlets and events business.
Beck also brings Franklin Covey leadership certification earned in both Indonesia and the Philippines, crisis management training, and speaks English, French and Spanish an asset for a hotel serving Dhaka's diverse corporate, diplomatic and leisure guests.
Commenting on the appointment, Hotel Sarina Dhaka expressed confidence that his international expertise and hands-on F&B leadership will strengthen the hotel's commercial performance, elevate guest experience across all outlets, and reinforce its position as one of Bangladesh's premier luxury hospitality destinations.
